subtitle: Six moves you'll use constantly — SQL's SELECT list and CASE WHEN, in pandas.

code:
o = orders.copy()
o["amount_with_tax"] = (o["amount"] * 1.08).round(2)

# order 1: 120.50 -> 130.14
# order 5 (missing amount): stays NaN
caption: Assign to a name that doesn't exist yet and pandas creates it — missing values propagate, no error.

code:
import numpy as np

o["size"] = np.where(o["amount"] >= 100, "large", "small")
caption: The pandas version of SQL's CASE WHEN for a two-way condition.

code:
conditions = [o["amount"] >= 200, o["amount"] >= 100]
np.select(conditions, ["big", "medium"], default="small")

# order 5 (NaN amount): NaN >= 100 is False -> "small" (wrong!)
caption: Checked in order, strictest first. A missing amount silently reads as "small" unless you handle isna() too.
Any value not in the dictionary becomes NaN — check your mapping covers everything.
Intervals are closed on the right by default — exactly 75 falls into "low".
rename and drop return a new DataFrame — they don't change o unless you assign the result back.
Works, but slower than vectorized math — prefer arithmetic, np.where, or map when they fit.

eyebrow: assign — and a copy warning to know
code:
orders.assign(amount_k=orders["amount"] / 1000)

sub = orders[orders["amount"] > 100].copy()  # avoids
sub["flag"] = 1                                # SettingWithCopyWarning
caption: assign chains a new column without touching the original; .copy() after filtering avoids the warning.
